_note: 1881-87 cities for the Western Canada (CPR) map. lat/lon are real modern coordinates for the historical site; name is the name IN USE 1881-87 (see docs/western-canada-board-research.md §5 for the period-name-trap checklist — Lethbridge and Vancouver are both accepted anachronisms for part of the window, kept per the locked design decision). full/shared are the two printed income values, tiered by role (capital/hub > CPR divisional point or documented construction-era population > construction camp/garrison/thin place) per docs/western-canada-board-research.md §1 and its explicit note that a Historical-Atlas-quality population ladder does not exist for this era. hub = non-developable (black square); the 5 locked hubs are Winnipeg, Calgary, Edmonton, Regina, Vancouver — NOT Victoria, which the research doc's own §2 recommends as a hub but the design's locked decision (see build task) overrides in favour of Edmonton+Regina. special = one of the 3 $10 connection cities (Winnipeg, Calgary, Vancouver). region is for terrain authoring and the research doc only.

cities.name: Winnipeg
cities.note: 7,985 at the 1881 census, up from 241 in 1871; secondary sources cite 20,000+ by 1886 (MEDIUM). CPR's construction HQ and the undisputed hub of the whole build — the highest sourced population figure on this board.

cities.name: St. Boniface
cities.note: French-Catholic/Métis settlement across the Red River from Winnipeg, founded 1818, Louis Riel's birthplace; administratively separate but geographically on top of Winnipeg (no era population figure found — kept low and, as flagged in the research doc, expected to need nudging away from Winnipeg the way Hamilton did on the Canadian board).
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: at the compressed 24x22 grid all 6 of Winnipeg's own hex neighbours are already occupied by other cities pushed up against the map's east edge (Selkirk, Portage la Prairie) or by Emerson (unnudged, real-world due south), so the real-world 'just across the river, practically touching' direction (due east) is not available at any distance — the east edge sits right at Winnipeg's own column. Moved south-southwest to the nearest hex that clears every other city (checked by a bearing-constrained nudge solver, not a blind search); a larger nudge than the original board needed, an expected consequence of tripling city density, not a geographic misread

cities.name: Portage la Prairie
cities.note: Roughly 1,000 population, with a land-boom peak reported at 3,500 by spring 1882 (a speculative bubble figure, not a stable count).
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: at 24x22 density this projects adjacent to Winnipeg (via Brandon's own real WNW line toward it); nudged further along that same real-world direction (west + north) until clear of Winnipeg, St. Boniface and Selkirk

cities.name: Brandon
cities.note: Chosen as a CPR divisional point spring 1881; population ~196 (1881) -> ~500 by year end -> 2,348 (1885); incorporated a city 1882, skipping town status entirely.

cities.name: Selkirk
cities.note: The originally-intended CPR crossing of the Red River (bridge opened June 1881) before the company switched the main line south through Winnipeg instead — a genuine 'what almost happened' story beat; no era population figure found.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: real-world Selkirk is NE of Winnipeg; nudged one hex further north along that same line to clear Winnipeg's own hex at 24x22 density

cities.name: Emerson
cities.note: Border town on the Pembina Branch (1878), the first railway to reach Manitoba, three years before the CPR mainline existed. No era population figure found — not invented.

cities.name: Regina
cities.note: Founded 1882 as a CPR townsite on Wascana Creek, chosen by the CPR itself; NWT territorial capital from 1883 (replacing Battleford) and NWMP HQ the same year. No hard in-era population figure exists (2,249 at the 1901 census is the first solid number) — valued for its unmatched administrative weight across the whole non-Manitoba, non-BC map, on par with the other capital-tier hubs.

cities.name: Battleford
cities.note: NWT's first capital 1876-1883, a NWMP fort of about ten buildings by 1880; lost capital status to Regina in 1883 specifically because Regina sat on the CPR main line and Battleford did not. Site of 1885 North-West Rebellion fighting (Fort Battleford). Valued for its displaced-capital political weight, not its garrison size.

cities.name: Prince Albert
cities.note: Founded 1866 as a Presbyterian mission; ~500 people at the mission by end of 1882, 'more than 5,000 in the area'. Capital of the District of Saskatchewan until 1905. Off the CPR main line, historically reachable only via the Qu'Appelle, Long Lake & Saskatchewan Railroad — a branch destination, not a mainline stop.

cities.name: Fort Qu'Appelle
cities.note: Continuously-operated HBC trading post since 1864, became the HBC's district headquarters in 1882 — a real, old, distinct place from the CPR's own Qu'Appelle Station 15 km away. No era population figure found.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: real-world Fort Qu'Appelle is north of Regina; at 24x22 density it lands hex-adjacent to Regina and Qu'Appelle Station both, so nudged one further hex north along the same real line

cities.name: Qu'Appelle Station
cities.note: Post office founded as 'Troy' 1 August 1882, renamed Qu'Appelle Station when the CPR arrived in 1884 (period-name trap: 'Troy' is correct 1882-84, this name 1884-87 — using the post-1884 CPR name per the task brief, matching how the board treats Vancouver/Lethbridge). A fire in 1883 destroyed much of the business district, implying real size before the rename.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: projects onto Regina's own hex at 24x22 density (the whole Qu'Appelle/Indian Head cluster is real-world within ~30km of Regina); nudged north-northwest, the closest direction that clears Regina, Fort Qu'Appelle, Indian Head and Moose Jaw all at once

cities.name: Indian Head
cities.note: Settlers arrived 1882 just ahead of the CPR; site of the 50,000+ acre 'Bell Farm' model farm — by June 1883 it had ~70 buildings including several stone structures.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: real-world Indian Head is due east of Regina; at 24x22 density it lands hex-adjacent to Regina and Fort Qu'Appelle, so nudged one further hex east along the same real line

cities.name: Moose Jaw
cities.note: Land speculators arrived 1881 anticipating a CPR divisional point; construction crews reached it 6 September 1882, first scheduled passenger train 1 April 1883. Population fluctuated 2,000-3,000 by May 1883 (a construction-boom figure); incorporated as a town 13 February 1884.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: real-world Moose Jaw is due west of Regina; at 24x22 density the direct route west is blocked by Swift Current's own hex footprint, so nudged further west along the same line until clear of both Regina and Swift Current

cities.name: Swift Current
cities.note: Townsite reserved early 1882 after the 1881 survey reached Swift Current Creek; became a divisional point for its reliable water. No population figure found for the era — genuinely thin.

cities.name: Maple Creek
cities.note: Townsite surveyed August 1883 alongside Calgary, Swift Current and Medicine Hat; became the NWMP's new divisional headquarters in 1883 after Fort Walsh closed. No population figure found.

cities.name: Calgary
cities.note: Originated as NWMP Fort Calgary (1875); the CPR reached it August 1883, choosing the southerly Kicking Horse Pass route over the assumed Yellowhead/Edmonton route. Incorporated a town 1884; a 'few hundred' settlers in 1883 growing to 3,876 at the 1891 census.

cities.name: Edmonton
cities.note: A real, continuously-occupied fur-trade settlement (Fort Edmonton), surveyed 1881 amid a small land rush when the CPR was still expected via the Yellowhead Pass. When the CPR chose the Kicking Horse/Calgary route instead, 'Edmonton's growth tailed off' and it was not reached by any railway until 1891 — after this board's window. Locked as a hub per the design brief despite this thin, deliberately modest value: a hub that pays less than several developable cities is an intentional echo of the real bypass story, flagged for the balance-measurement phase in case it proves unbuildable-into in practice.

cities.name: Fort Macleod
cities.note: First permanent NWMP post in the far west (October 1874), garrison of ~10 officers/140 constables; rebuilt 1884. A garrison, not a settled town, through this era.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: real-world Fort Macleod is west of Lethbridge; at 24x22 density the immediate hex west is already occupied by the Calgary/mountain cluster's own satellites, so nudged one hex further west along the same real line

cities.name: Lethbridge
cities.note: Period-name trap: called 'Coalbanks' until October 1885, when it was renamed Lethbridge (after the coal company's president) — 'Lethbridge' is only accurate for the last ~2 years of the board's window. Kept as 'Lethbridge' per the task brief (matches how the board treats Vancouver's own, larger anachronism). North Western Coal and Navigation Company mine from October 1882; population 'over 1,000' by end of 1885.

cities.name: Cochrane
cities.note: Cochrane Ranche, Alberta's first large-scale ranch (1881-88, Senator Matthew Cochrane); represents the ranching economy the CPR's arrival opened up, not a town as such.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: real-world Cochrane is NW of Calgary; at 24x22 density it projects onto Calgary's own hex, so nudged along that same NW line until clear

cities.name: Banff
cities.note: Hot springs discovered by CPR railway workers in 1883; the Banff Hot Springs Reserve was created 25 Nov 1885 to settle a commercial dispute, expanded as Rocky Mountains Park by the 23 June 1887 Act. Essentially no in-era population — a federal reserve, not a town, but excellent story colour worth a low-but-present value rather than exclusion.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: real-world Banff is NW of Calgary but the direct NW line is boxed in by Field/Golden/Cochrane's own hexes at this density; nudged west and south instead (the next-best available direction) to clear Calgary, Cochrane and Golden all at once

cities.name: Gleichen
cities.note: Named by the CPR in 1883 (previously 'Twelfth Siding') after Count Gleichen, a CPR financial backer; became a divisional point with a roundhouse. No population figure found.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: real-world Gleichen is east (and slightly south) of Calgary; at 24x22 density it projects hex-adjacent to Calgary, so nudged one further hex east along that line

cities.name: Medicine Hat
cities.note: The CPR reached it in 1883 to bridge the South Saskatchewan River; began as a construction tent town and became a CPR divisional point (incorporated only in 1898).

cities.name: Vancouver
cities.note: Period-name trap, the biggest on the board: named 'Granville' (also 'Gastown') for almost this entire window, renamed Vancouver only on incorporation 6 April 1886 at Van Horne's insistence. Kept as 'Vancouver' per the already-locked design decision (accurate only for the last ~18 months of the era). Chosen over Port Moody as the permanent Pacific terminus; the first transcontinental train reached it 23 May 1887.

cities.name: New Westminster
cities.note: The real colonial capital of the mainland (1859-1868) before Victoria was chosen; the leading mainland city in the 1880s on salmon canning and lumber, before Vancouver's post-1886 rise eclipsed it. No specific era population figure found — not invented.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: the Lower Mainland cluster (Vancouver/Port Moody/New Westminster) is a genuinely tight real-world triangle (~15-20 km on a side) that projects onto Vancouver's own hex at 24x22 density; New Westminster is real-world upriver/south-east of Vancouver, so nudged that direction, clear of Vancouver, Port Moody and Yale

cities.name: Port Moody
cities.note: Named the CPR's western terminus in 1879; station built 1882; a land boom followed the first construction steel in March 1883. Received the actual first transcontinental passenger train, 4 July 1886 — ten months before Vancouver took over that role. A genuine 'boomed, then bypassed' story.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: the Lower Mainland cluster projects onto Vancouver's own hex at 24x22 density; Port Moody is real-world east of Vancouver (across Burrard Inlet), so nudged due east, clear of Vancouver, New Westminster and Yale

cities.name: Yale
cities.note: Headquarters and supply depot for Andrew Onderdonk's Fraser Canyon contract, 1880-85, coordinating roughly 7,000 workers (many Chinese labourers recruited specifically for this work). Population collapsed sharply once construction finished in 1885 — a boom/bust curve, not a stable count.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: at 24x22 density Yale projects hex-adjacent to Vancouver; real-world Yale is upriver (further inland/north-east along the Fraser) from Vancouver, so nudged north to clear it

cities.name: Kamloops
cities.note: Construction reached it in 1883; through-service from 1885/86. Genuinely small through this whole era — incorporated only in 1893 with a population of roughly 500. Kept explicitly thin rather than padded.

cities.name: Revelstoke
cities.note: Surveyed as 'Farwell' in 1885, renamed Revelstoke in 1886 after Lord Revelstoke, the British financier whose firm helped underwrite CPR construction finance. Barely exists before 1885.

cities.name: Golden
cities.note: Emerged as a construction tent town in 1884-85 at the Kicking Horse/Columbia River junction; was originally intended as the mountain divisional point (a role that went to Revelstoke only in 1899). Tiny population in-era.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: real-world Golden is WSW of Field, but at 24x22 density the whole Field-Banff-Cochrane-Revelstoke pileup boxes in every hex within 2 steps of that direct line; nudged further southwest, the nearest hex a bearing-constrained solver found clear of all four neighbours -- a bigger nudge than the rest of this cluster needed, a direct consequence of the mountain corridor's real-world density, not an arbitrary placement

cities.name: Field
cities.note: CPR station near the base of the Kicking Horse Pass 'Big Hill' grade, established during mid-1880s mountain-section construction.

cities.name: Victoria
cities.note: Capital of the united Colony of British Columbia since 1866, and of the province since 1871; population 5,925 at the 1881 census — the largest hard population figure of any place in this whole research doc after Winnipeg. NOT a locked hub on this board (the design brief overrides the research doc's own hub recommendation in favour of Edmonton+Regina) — valued high as a developable city instead, on the logic used repeatedly on the Canadian board that a remote, high-value prize justifies the cost of the spur (here, the Vancouver Island water-gap crossing) that reaches it.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: kept south down-island of Nanaimo, same as the original board, but the rescaled grid's rows 18-21 exist specifically to give this cluster room (see project.mjs) -- Victoria sits 2 hexes south of Nanaimo, mirroring how far down-island it sits in reality relative to the Nanaimo-Vancouver crossing point

cities.name: Esquimalt
cities.note: Royal Navy's Pacific Station headquarters since 1865; the Esquimalt & Nanaimo Railway reached it in 1886 and the naval dockyard was completed in 1887. No standalone population figure found (folded into greater Victoria in most sources).
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: projects onto the same hex as Victoria (they are real, adjoining neighbours, ~5 km apart in reality). A straight south nudge needs 4 rows of clearance at this density and pushes the whole island cluster into the printed company-plates strip at the bottom of the frame, so shifted east instead (2 hexes east, same row as Victoria) -- enough hex distance to clear Victoria and New Westminster both while keeping the whole island within the board's vertical budget

cities.name: Nanaimo
cities.note: HBC coal operation since 1852; grew from ~1,000 (1874) toward ~10,000 by 1900 — no single figure pinned to 1881-87 specifically, so this value is an interpolated mid-era estimate, not a sourced fact for this exact window.
cities.nudgeWhy: RESCALE: Vancouver Island is physically separate from the mainland (see terrain.json's water-gap region). Shifted 2 hexes south of its raw projected position -- which otherwise lands 2 hexes due west of Vancouver at the SAME row, i.e. would read as ordinary adjacent mainland rather than an island across a strait. The 2-hex south shift plus the off-map hexes hand-carved into terrain.json puts exactly one land hex, (1,16), between Nanaimo and Vancouver: a real, single-tile bridge crossing, not a wide land connection -- see docs/western-canada-board-rescale-final.md for the exact hex-by-hex reasoning
